parts.title: Oil, Power and Conflict: Baku after the October Revolution
parts.passage_html:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

A When the Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd on 25 October (7 November) 1917, Transcaucasia responded in two opposite ways. In Tiflis, the Georgian Mensheviks, the Azerbaijani Musavat party and the Armenian Dashnaktsutyun refused to recognise Lenin's government, and on 15 (28) November they created a provisional regional authority, the Transcaucasian Commissariat, chaired by Evgeni Gegechkori. The new body was fragile from the start: it had no army of its own and depended on the national councils for troops. Baku, however, took a different path. As the only large city in the region with a substantial Russian and Armenian industrial working class, it recognised the Soviet government.

B The Bolsheviks' difficulty was that they enjoyed little popular support. In the elections to the All-Russian Constituent Assembly in November 1917, Musavat won roughly 616,000 votes in Transcaucasia, while the Bolsheviks received only about 4 per cent. Even in Baku the pattern was similar: in the October 1917 elections to the city's Soviet, Musavat took almost 40 per cent of some 25,000 votes, whereas the Bolsheviks attracted close to 4,000. The historian Kazemzadeh, writing in 1951, concluded that 'the national factor largely determined the way a person voted'. Musavat nevertheless declined to take up its seats, and when most other parties walked out, a rump Soviet dominated by Bolsheviks and Left Socialist Revolutionaries remained, with Stepan Shaumyan as its chairman.

C Lacking votes, the Soviet needed force. In December 1917 Lenin appointed Shaumyan Extraordinary Commissar for the Caucasus, and a Red Guard was formed, yet the Soviet's own troops remained weak. The strongest armed body in the city belonged to the Dashnaks, whose units had bought weapons from Russian soldiers deserting the collapsing Caucasian front. The Azerbaijanis, by contrast, had arms but, in Kazemzadeh's words, 'no comparable organization or experience': under the Tsar, Muslims had been exempt from conscription, so the community had almost no trained officers. By late January 1918 a Bolshevik newspaper was describing Baku as divided into 'two large enemy camps', Musavat and Dashnaktsutyun, and warning that 'a clash is inevitable'.

D The clash came at the end of March 1918. On 30 March the Soviet disarmed the Muslim crew of the ship Evelina, claiming that they were preparing a revolt, although Kazemzadeh states that this report 'lacked foundation'. When Muslims gathered to demand the return of the weapons, shooting broke out. On 31 March the Soviet issued an ultimatum requiring recognition of its authority, the withdrawal of the Muslim 'Savage Division' and the reopening of the railways. At this point the Armenian National Council, which had previously declared itself neutral, joined the Soviet, and ships of the Caspian fleet shelled the Muslim quarters. Although Musavat accepted the ultimatum on 1 April, the killing of civilians continued until the fighting ended on 2 April.

E The scale of the losses remains disputed, and historians are careful to state whose figures they use. Shaumyan reported to Moscow that 'more than three thousand' people had died on both sides and described the results as 'brilliant'. The Azerbaijani delegation to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, by contrast, put the number of victims at more than twelve thousand, many of them old men, women and children. The Ismailiyya building and the offices of the newspaper Kaspi were burned, the Taza Pir mosque was damaged by shells, and tens of thousands of Muslims fled the city. Kazemzadeh's interpretation is that the Soviet provoked a 'civil war' in order to break its most formidable rival, but that once it had called on the Dashnaks for help, the conflict 'degenerated into a massacre'.

F On 25 April 1918 the Bolsheviks formalised their rule by creating the Baku Council of People's Commissars, known as the Baku Commune. It closed the City Duma, banned opposition newspapers and, in June, nationalised the oil industry. Lenin had already assigned 100 million roubles to pay Baku's workers and buy oil for Russia, which shows how much the city's fuel mattered to Moscow. Meanwhile, the Commune's detachments, largely Dashnak in composition, carried the violence into districts such as Shamakhi, Guba, Lankaran and Salyan. An Extraordinary Investigation Commission, set up by the government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic (ADR) on 15 July 1918, gathered 36 volumes of evidence. Azerbaijani historians draw heavily on this material, although its figures cover different periods and perpetrators, and the cases were eventually dropped under an amnesty in February 1920.

G The Commune's decline was rapid. In June its army advanced on Ganja, the temporary capital of the newly independent ADR, but between 27 June and 1 July it was defeated at Goychay by the Caucasian Islamic Army of Nuri Pasha. The Commune resigned on 31 July, and the Centrocaspian Dictatorship that replaced it invited a British force of about 1,000 men. On 15 September 1918 the Islamic Army liberated Baku. Reprisals against Armenians followed, and a commission of the Armenian National Council counted 8,988 dead; the ADR government formally condemned these killings.

H The events of 1918 had lasting political consequences, destroying Azerbaijani faith in autonomy within Russia and pushing the national movement towards independence, declared on 28 May 1918. Their interpretation, however, has varied. Soviet historians presented March as a struggle of the Baku proletariat against Musavat 'counter-revolution' and celebrated the 26 Baku Commissars as heroes. Since 1991 Azerbaijani historians have described the events as a planned genocide by the Bolshevik-Dashnak alliance, while the Western scholar Swietochowski regarded the March Days as the decisive turning point towards Azerbaijani independence. In 1998 a presidential decree established 31 March as the Day of Genocide of Azerbaijanis.

parts.title: From Faction to State: Azerbaijani Deputies in the Transcaucasian Seym
parts.passage_html:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

A Between February and May 1918, Transcaucasia changed from a province of a collapsing Russia into three separate republics, and the Muslim deputies of the Transcaucasian Seym played a central part in this transformation. The Seym itself was an improvisation. The regional leaders in Tiflis had hoped that the All-Russian Constituent Assembly would restore a democratic Russia, but when the Bolsheviks dispersed it in January 1918, they decided to set up a parliament of their own. No new elections were held. Instead, the Transcaucasian results of the Constituent Assembly elections were reused, and the number of votes needed to win a seat was cut to one third, so that every party sent roughly three times as many deputies as before.

B The Seym opened in Tiflis on 10 (23) February 1918 under the Georgian Menshevik Nikolay Chkheidze. Although about ten parties were represented, Kazemzadeh, the Western historian who wrote the standard account in 1951, observed that 'in reality it was composed of the representatives of the three major ethnic groups'. The Georgian Mensheviks and Musavat held about 30 seats each and the Armenian Dashnaktsutyun 27. Together with the Muslim Socialist Bloc, Hummat and Ittihad, the Muslim faction numbered 44 deputies, led by figures such as Mammad Amin Rasulzade, Fatali khan Khoyski, Nasib bey Yusifbeyli and Mammad Hasan Hajinski. The Bolsheviks boycotted the new parliament.

C Questions of war and peace dominated the Seym from the outset, and on these the Muslim deputies took a distinctive line. On 1 March they joined a unanimous vote that peace should be made with Turkey on the basis of the 1914 borders. Two days later, however, Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, which handed Kars, Ardahan and Batum to the Ottoman Empire. The Georgian and Armenian majority refused to recognise the treaty, but Khoyski pointed out the inconsistency of acting as part of Russia one day and rejecting a Russian treaty the next. When news of the March massacres in Baku reached the Seym, Rasulzade demanded immediate help for the city and threatened a Muslim boycott. In mid-April, as the Seym voted for war with Turkey, Shafi bey Rustambeyli declared that Azerbaijanis would not fight their co-religionists, and the Musavat benches stayed empty until midnight.

D Peace talks had opened at Trabzon on 14 March. The Transcaucasian delegation, headed by the Georgian Akaki Chkhenkeli, included Hajinski among its Muslim members, while the Ottoman side, led by Rauf Bey, insisted on the Brest-Litovsk terms. On 20 March the Ottomans called on Transcaucasia to proclaim its independence, arguing that a territory which had been part of Russia when the treaty was signed had no legal ground to reject it, a position Kazemzadeh considers 'legally correct'. Each nationality had its own priority: the Georgians would not give up Batum, the Armenians would not surrender Kars, and the Azerbaijanis wanted peace and independence. Chkhenkeli accepted Brest-Litovsk on 10 April, but Tiflis recalled the delegation and declared war; Hajinski kept negotiating with the Ottomans regardless. Batum soon fell, and on 22 April the Seym proclaimed the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic, in whose cabinet Azerbaijanis received five posts.

E The federation lasted barely a month. At the Batum conference, which opened on 11 May, the Ottoman delegation under Halil Bey and Vehib Pasha demanded more than Brest-Litovsk had given, including Akhaltsikhe, Akhalkalaki and Alexandropol. The German general von Lossow, who attended as an observer, offered mediation, an idea the Armenian delegates welcomed. Hajinski objected, arguing that a few territorial concessions would not hurt Transcaucasia, and an Armenian delegate openly accused him of passing information to the Turks. On 21 May Azerbaijani leaders proposed that, if the federation collapsed, they would accept at least a 'dual state' with Georgia, but the Georgians refused and secretly reached an agreement with Germany instead. On 26 May Georgia declared independence and the Seym dissolved itself.

F The Muslim faction moved quickly. On 27 May its 44 deputies formed the Azerbaijani National Council, with Rasulzade as chairman, and the next day the Council adopted the Declaration of Independence. This proclaimed a democratic republic that guaranteed civil and political rights to all citizens regardless of nationality, religion, social position or sex. Khoyski formed the first government, and nearly all its ministers had sat in the Seym's Muslim faction. On 4 June Rasulzade and Hajinski signed the Treaty of Batum with the Ottoman Empire. Its fourth article promised Ottoman military assistance on request, which became the legal basis for the Caucasian Islamic Army that liberated Baku on 15 September 1918. In mid-June, after the Georgian government asked the Azerbaijani bodies to leave Tiflis, the government moved to Ganja, its temporary capital.

G Historians remain divided over how to judge the faction's conduct. Kazemzadeh, whose account draws on Georgian émigré sources, argued that the Azerbaijanis were 'closer to the enemy than to the state of which they formed a part'. Yet he also acknowledged that their motive was Baku rather than religion, noting that Shiite Azerbaijanis had fought Sunni Ottomans for centuries. Swietochowski saw the deputies as pragmatists who needed an outside protector after the Baku massacres, while Azerbaijani historians regard the Seym as the school of national parliamentarism from which the first parliamentary republic in the Muslim East emerged.

parts.title: A Nation Finds Its Voice: Azerbaijan in 1917
parts.passage_html:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

A The February Revolution of 1917 swept away the Tsarist autocracy that had governed northern Azerbaijan for about a century. When the news reached Baku and Tiflis in the first days of March, the police and the old administration simply disappeared, and Azerbaijanis enjoyed freedom of speech, of the press and of organisation for the first time. The eight months that followed were marked by political freedom, divided authority and a deepening economic crisis. They were also the period in which the Azerbaijani national movement was transformed from a collection of scattered intellectual circles into a mass movement with a clear programme.

B Authority in the region was fragmented. On 9 March the Provisional Government created the Special Transcaucasian Committee, known as OZAKOM, in Tiflis. Chaired by V. A. Kharlamov and composed of Duma members, among them the Azerbaijani Mammad Yusif Jafarov, it took over civil administration from the viceroy but had no legislative power. The historian Firuz Kazemzadeh dismisses it as 'a collective Viceroy, only much weaker'. In Baku, meanwhile, two bodies claimed authority. The Executive Committee of Public Organizations brought together the City Duma, the oil industrialists and various national groups, while the Baku Soviet of Workers' Deputies, which first met on 6 March with 52 delegates, was dominated by Socialist Revolutionaries and Mensheviks. Although the Bolsheviks held only two or three seats, their leader Stepan Shaumyan was elected chairman in his absence.

C Azerbaijani workers were weakly represented in the Soviet, which many Azerbaijanis came to regard as an institution belonging to 'others'. Instead, they built organisations of their own. In Baku a Provisional Committee of Muslim Public Organizations was set up, headed by Ali Mardan bey Topchubashov, a lawyer and former member of the First Duma, with Mammad Amin Rasulzade among its leading figures. Similar Muslim National Councils appeared in Ganja and in district towns, where they functioned as a national government in miniature, organising meetings, collecting money, running schools and representing Muslims before the authorities. The Baku committee declared that the only acceptable form of government for Russia was a democratic republic.

D The national programme took shape at a series of congresses. The Caucasian Muslim Congress, held in Baku from 15 to 20 April, called for universal free education in the Azerbaijani language, but its most important decisions were military: a census of Muslim military potential and the creation of bureaus to organise Muslim detachments. This mattered because Azerbaijanis, unlike Armenians and Georgians, had never been conscripted into the Russian army and therefore had almost no trained soldiers. A few weeks later, at the First All-Russian Muslim Congress in Moscow, some 900 delegates debated the future of Russia's Muslims. The Volga Tatars favoured a single Russia with cultural autonomy for all Muslims, whereas Rasulzade led those demanding territorial autonomy for each nation within a democratic federal republic. His resolution won by 446 votes to 271, establishing the idea that Azerbaijan was a distinct territorial nation rather than simply part of a wider Muslim community.

E Political parties now operated openly. In June the Baku party Musavat merged with the Turkic Party of Federalists, founded in Ganja by Nasib bey Yusifbeyli, to form the Turkic Federalist Party Musavat. According to Tadeusz Swietochowski, the new party consisted of two distinct wings, a Left based in Baku and a Right based in Ganja, which disagreed on social questions, especially land, but were held together by secular Turkic nationalism. Not every group shared this vision. The Pan-Islamist party Ittihad opposed territorial autonomy because it would divide the Muslim community, and the socialist Hummat, led by Nariman Narimanov, rejected it as well.

F Economic hardship formed the background to these developments. Between the outbreak of war and January 1917, prices rose by about 350 per cent, while wages increased by only about 200 per cent; in 1916 alone, meat became 142 per cent more expensive. Baku, which supplied most of Russia's oil, had a multinational population in which Azerbaijanis made up only about 21 per cent in 1913, and its skilled workforce was largely non-Azerbaijani. Strikes for an eight-hour day led to a collective agreement in May, and a general strike in the oil industry followed in September.

G The strength of the national movement became evident at the ballot box. In the October elections to the Baku Soviet, Musavat received almost 10,000 of about 25,000 votes, roughly 40 per cent and more than any other party, while the Bolsheviks gained around 4,000. Kazemzadeh concluded that 'the national factor largely determined the way a person voted'. Yet Musavat chose not to enter the Soviet, which was left in the hands of the Bolsheviks and their allies, a decision Kazemzadeh calls 'a blunder for which they were destined to pay dearly'. In the Constituent Assembly elections held the following month, Musavat won about 63 per cent of the Muslim vote in Transcaucasia.

H Most historians accept that the national idea reached the majority of Azerbaijanis in 1917, but they interpret its significance differently. Later Soviet writers portrayed Musavat as a 'counter-revolutionary' party of beks and khans, although the early Soviet author A. L. Popov admitted that it had stood on the positions of democracy and even socialism. Kazemzadeh regarded the whole period as 'only a prelude to greater struggles', while Swietochowski described it as 'the transition toward nationhood'. What is clear is that the goal remained autonomy within a federal Russia rather than independence; only the events of the following months would push the movement towards the independent republic proclaimed on 28 May 1918.

groups.content_html:
National organisations and parties in 1917

Many Azerbaijanis saw the Baku Soviet as a body that belonged to other groups, so they formed their own organisations. In Baku, Topchubashov headed a committee of Muslim organisations, while in Ganja and smaller towns Muslim National Councils acted as a national government in {{31}}. In June, Musavat united with a party from Ganja; the resulting party had two {{32}} which disagreed about land but were bound together by secular Turkic {{33}}. Not everyone supported territorial autonomy: it was opposed both by Ittihad, a {{34}} party, and by the socialists of Hummat. All this took place against a background of economic hardship, as prices had risen far faster than {{35}} since the start of the war.

Similar Muslim National Councils appeared in Ganja and in district towns, where they functioned as a national government in miniature, organising meetings, collecting money, running schools and representing Muslims before the authorities.

questions.prompt_html: The Tsarist police remained active in Baku for some weeks after news of the revolution arrived.
questions.explanation_html:
Answer Explanation:

The passage says that when the news arrived the police and the old administration 'simply disappeared', which contradicts the statement.

Evidence from the passage:

When the news reached Baku and Tiflis in the first days of March, the police and the old administration simply disappeared, and Azerbaijanis enjoyed freedom of speech, of the press and of organisation for the first time.

questions.prompt_html: Rasulzade had prepared his resolution together with the Bashkir delegates.
questions.explanation_html:
Answer Explanation:

The passage says Rasulzade led the supporters of territorial autonomy and that his resolution won, but it does not say who helped him prepare it or mention Bashkir delegates.

Evidence from the passage:

The Volga Tatars favoured a single Russia with cultural autonomy for all Muslims, whereas Rasulzade led those demanding territorial autonomy for each nation within a democratic federal republic.

questions.prompt_html: In 1913 Azerbaijanis were a minority of the population of Baku.
questions.explanation_html:
Answer Explanation:

Azerbaijanis made up only about 21 per cent of Baku's population in 1913, i.e. a minority.

Evidence from the passage:

Baku, which supplied most of Russia's oil, had a multinational population in which Azerbaijanis made up only about 21 per cent in 1913, and its skilled workforce was largely non-Azerbaijani.

questions.prompt_html: In the October elections to the Baku Soviet, the Bolsheviks won more than half as many votes as Musavat.
questions.explanation_html:
Answer Explanation:

Musavat received almost 10,000 votes and the Bolsheviks around 4,000, which is less than half of Musavat's total.

Evidence from the passage:

In the October elections to the Baku Soviet, Musavat received almost 10,000 of about 25,000 votes, roughly 40 per cent and more than any other party, while the Bolsheviks gained around 4,000.
